planting.note: Fall-sow seed outdoors to satisfy a cold-moist stratification requirement, or plant container stock in spring or fall into rocky, alkaline, very well-drained soil; seedlings and young plants need protection from rabbits.

directions: Plant in full sun in rocky, lean, alkaline, fast-draining soil typical of pinyon-juniper slopes and mesa rims across the Four Corners region; cliffrose is intolerant of heavy clay or regular irrigation once established. Small cream to pale-yellow five-petaled flowers cover the gray-green, deeply lobed leaves in late spring, followed by distinctive feathery plumed seed tails similar to its close relative Apache plume. Established plants are extremely drought- and heat-tolerant and provide critical winter browse for deer and bighorn sheep. Avoid summer watering, which encourages root rot in this high-desert evergreen shrub.

planting.note: Direct-sow in fall for natural stratification, or set out container plants in spring; use coarse, fast-draining sandy or rocky soil and avoid overwatering young plants.

directions: Plant in full sun in dry, rocky or sandy, well-drained soil typical of pinyon-juniper woodland and sagebrush flats across the Colorado Plateau. This leafless, broom-like shrub photosynthesizes through its slender, bright green jointed stems and bears small yellow cone-like strobili at the stem joints in spring on separate male and female plants. Extremely drought-tolerant once established and nearly maintenance-free, it has long been harvested by Southwestern tribes and settlers to brew a mild, caffeine-free herbal tea from the dried stems. Needs no supplemental water beyond establishment and resents soggy or amended soil.

planting.note: Direct-sow seed or set out container plants in spring into gritty, fast-draining soil; established clumps spread slowly by rhizome and rarely need division.

directions: Grow in full sun in sandy or rocky, very well-drained soil on open flats and slopes among pinyon-juniper and sagebrush of the Colorado Plateau. Narrowleaf yucca forms low, clustering rosettes of thin, curling-fibered gray-green leaves and sends up a sparse flower stalk to about three feet bearing creamy white, bell-shaped blossoms in late spring to early summer. It is one of the hardiest and smallest-statured yuccas native to the Four Corners region, tolerating winter temperatures well below zero. Keep soil on the dry side year-round; excess moisture, especially in winter, causes crown rot.

planting.note: Fall-sow seed outdoors for winter cold-moist stratification, or set out nursery transplants in spring into gritty, fast-draining soil; self-sows readily once established in sandy sites.

directions: Plant in full sun in sandy, fast-draining soil, echoing the red-rock slickrock and sandy washes of the Colorado Plateau where this species is endemic. Narrow, waxy blue-green basal leaves give rise to upright spikes of vivid coral-pink to red tubular flowers in late spring, a favorite of hummingbirds migrating through canyon country. Like most rock-garden penstemons it is short-lived in heavy or rich soil but persists for years in lean, gritty conditions with sharp winter drainage. Avoid mulch against the crown and skip supplemental summer water once established.

planting.note: Fall-sow to break the hard seed coat over winter, or scarify seed before spring sowing; direct-sow into lean, well-drained soil since globemallows resent transplanting once taprooted.

directions: Grow in full sun in dry, rocky or sandy, alkaline soil typical of the shale and sandstone benches of the Colorado Plateau among pinyon-juniper and sagebrush. Grayish, gooseberry-like lobed leaves support loose spikes of apricot-orange, hibiscus-shaped flowers from spring into early summer, attracting native bees and globemallow bee specialists. It is a tough, deep-taprooted perennial that rebounds reliably after wildfire and disturbance, but it dislikes rich garden soil and regular watering, which shorten its lifespan. Deadhead spent stalks to tidy plants, but avoid heavy pruning into old wood.

planting.note: Fall-sow seed outdoors for cold stratification, or set out container stock in spring or fall into lean, rocky or clay-shale soil typical of badlands and mesa slopes.

directions: Plant in full sun in dry, rocky, clay-shale, or sandy alkaline soil found on the barren-looking slopes and benches of the Colorado Plateau, where it is a dominant late-season nectar source. Narrow, wavy-margined gray leaves form a woody-based clump topped by flat-headed clusters of cream to yellow flowers that turn rust-orange in late summer and fall, well after most Southwest wildflowers have finished. It is an exceptionally drought-tolerant subshrub that supports migrating butterflies and native bees when little else is blooming in high-desert gardens. Leave old flowering stems through winter for seed-eating birds, and avoid rich soil or extra irrigation, which shorten its life.

planting.note: Fall-sow fresh seed outdoors for winter cold-moist stratification, or plant container stock in spring or fall into rocky, alkaline, fast-draining soil; slow to establish but long-lived once rooted in.

directions: Plant in full sun to very light shade in rocky, alkaline, well-drained soil typical of canyon walls and mesa slopes of the Colorado Plateau and Great Basin. Stiff, holly-like, blue-gray compound leaves give this large evergreen shrub a striking desert-adapted look, with fragrant yellow flower clusters in early spring followed by dry, mealy red-brown berries relished by birds and once eaten by Native peoples. It is far more drought- and heat-tolerant than the familiar Oregon grape, thriving on summer heat and winter cold with minimal irrigation once established. Avoid heavy clay, regular watering, or dense shade, all of which weaken this high-desert native.

planting.note: Fall-sow seed outdoors or set out container plants in spring into lean, well-drained soil; germinates and establishes readily, often self-sowing along disturbed roadsides and washes.

directions: Plant in full sun in dry, rocky, sandy, or alkaline soil typical of open flats and disturbed ground within and bordering pinyon-juniper woodland across the Colorado Plateau and Great Basin. Narrow gray-green felted leaves and flexible stems support dense, rounded masses of bright golden-yellow flower clusters from late summer into fall, making it one of the last and most important nectar sources for migrating butterflies and native bees before frost. This fast-growing, short-lived subshrub tolerates extreme heat, cold, drought, and poor soil, and is commonly used for post-fire and roadside restoration as well as xeriscape pollinator gardens. Cut back hard in late winter every few years to keep plants dense, since older stems become woody and sparse.
